subject: Climate & Environment
title: Agroforestry: Farms and Trees Together
description: A short lesson to help you apply Agroforestry: Farms and Trees Together.

hook.text: What if farmers didn't have to choose between crops and trees?

buildup.text: Agroforestry mixes trees with crops or livestock on the same land.

discovery.text: Shade from trees reduces heat stress on crops and livestock, boosting productivity.

twist.text: Tree roots pull nutrients from deep soil layers that crops can't reach on their own.

climax.text: Agroforestry sequesters carbon, prevents erosion, and increases farmer income.

punchline.text: The farm of the future has trees in it, not around it.

quiz.question: What is agroforestry?
options: Mixing trees with crops or livestock on the same land

details.summary: Agroforestry integrates trees with crops or livestock on the same land, combining agricultural production with environmental benefits. It can increase yields, improve soil health, sequester carbon, and provide additional income from fruit, timber, or nuts.
details.whyItMatters: Agroforestry offers a way to produce food while restoring tree cover, making it a bridge between agriculture and conservation that benefits farmers and ecosystems.
takeaways: Shade trees can increase coffee and cocoa yields and quality
Tree roots reduce erosion and improve water infiltration on farms
Agroforestry stores 2 to 10 times more carbon than conventional farming

faq.question: How does agroforestry benefit farmers economically?
faq.answer: Trees provide fruit, nuts, fodder, timber, and firewood alongside crop income. They buffer against price swings through diversification, improve soil fertility reducing fertilizer costs, and provide shade that protects crops and livestock from heat stress.

faq.question: Is agroforestry widely practiced?
faq.answer: An estimated 1.2 billion people practice some form of agroforestry worldwide, especially in tropical smallholder systems. It is expanding as climate-smart agriculture gains attention, but formalized adoption in industrial farming systems remains limited.
